# Control Your DAW with this Rock-Solid Roland Sequencer

> **Stage:** Outlining — this document is the outline. On approve, it gets snapshotted to `scrapbook/outline.md` and `index.md` gets rewritten as the draft body.

## Frame (audience + register)

This is a dispatch for **musicians**, not software engineers. Operator's note in the v4 review: *"No one cares about the code. We don't want to talk about the code at all. This is for musicians, not software engineers."*

That cuts a lot of v5's draft outline:

- No ASCII diagram. Musicians won't read it.
- No "implementation callout" with SPP / MCU / MTC / CoreMIDI. No protocol-speak in the prose at all. (One opt-in pointer at the end for curious readers, but not a paragraph.)
- No Homebrew tap name. That's documentation, not a blog post.
- No "hard problem" framing. The hook is enthusiasm: *how cool would it be if you could use this great vintage device with your DAW.*

What stays: the journey from "two great things that couldn't talk" to "two great things that go great together," anchored in the audiocontrol mission — modern tooling for great vintage gear.

## Hero placement

**Demo video moves above the fold.** First thing the reader sees after the dek. Operator's v4 note: *"Put above the fold."*

Embed: <https://youtu.be/IIhBlliWr9k>

The dispatch's payoff is the video. The reader watches the MC-500mkII drive LUNA's transport in the first ten seconds, *then* reads why this matters.

## Working title

**Picked:** *Control Your DAW with this Rock-Solid Roland Sequencer*

Reasoning: operator's direction in v1's review (*"rock-solid"* is the VO callback — *"It's rock solid, feels great"*) and v4's title comment. "This Roland Sequencer" reads conversationally — the reader doesn't need to swallow `MC-500mkII` in the title; the model number gets named in §01 once context is established.

Alts (kept in case operator wants to swap):

1. *Two Great Things That Couldn't Talk* (literary; needs SEO subtitle)
2. *The MC-500mkII Was Already Great. Now It Drives Your DAW.* (audiocontrol two-sentence-claim signature)
3. *From the Shelf to the Session: The MC-500mkII as DAW Transport*
4. *Hit Play on a 1988 Sequencer. Watch Logic Roll.*

## Dek (one sentence)

The Roland MC-500mkII has the best transport buttons in your studio. Your DAW has the takes. A small bridge makes the MC-500's panel — its buttons, its wheel, its 99 location memories — drive the modern session.

(Three sentences but reads as one beat. Short, short, payoff.)

## Section structure

Six sections (down from seven — the implementation callout and ASCII diagram are gone). Magazine dividers (`---`) between in the rendered article. Sentence-case headings. Demo video above the fold; sections build the narrative from there.

### § 01 — How cool would it be if...

Open with the *desire*, not the dissonance. *I've got this rock-solid 1988 Roland sequencer on a stand next to my desk. The transport buttons feel like flight hardware. The data wheel turns with real weight. It runs my MIDI takes from the same panel it ran them from when George H. W. Bush was president. And it sits there, doing its job, while I drive my DAW with the laptop trackpad. How cool would it be if the buttons just... ran the DAW.*

Two short paragraphs after that:

- The MC-500mkII (1988) — what it is, briefly. Multitrack recorder for MIDI. Best buttons in the studio. Speaks the language it spoke in 1988.
- Your DAW — Logic, Live, LUNA, whichever you live in. Speaks 2026's language.

Close: *I built a way to make them work together.*

### § 02 — What it actually does (musician-language)

Operator's framing (v4): *"a way to use the MC-500mkII (and, likely, related Roland sequencers from that era) as a control surface for your DAW."*

Plain language version: *the MC-500's panel becomes a hardware controller for your DAW. Something you already own. Something that sits beautifully on the desk. The buttons your fingers already know.*

**Screenshot placeholder:** the control surface / configuration interface in this section. Operator's v4 note: *"We need a screenshot of the control interface in this section."* (Image to be captured at draft time and dropped at `./control-interface.png` or similar.)

You hit play on the MC-500 — the DAW plays. You spin the wheel — the DAW jogs to where you want. You recall a location — the DAW seeks. That's the dispatch.

### § 03 — What you get from the panel

Transport buttons drive the DAW transport. Data wheel becomes the jog wheel. The 99 location memories become jump-to-marker buttons.

The location memories are the part most people will stop and reread. Pre-configure verse, chorus, bridge as MC-500 locations. Now one button on the panel jumps the DAW to that bar. The MC-500's panel becomes a tactile arrangement-jumping interface for whatever DAW is on the other end. Years of muscle memory finally pay rent.

### § 04 — The moment it works

The video already played above the fold. This section is the prose companion.

What you watched: the MC-500mkII driving LUNA. Hit play on the box, LUNA plays. Spin the wheel, LUNA jogs. Recall a location, LUNA seeks. Pull a quote from the VO inline:

> *"hit play on the MC-500, and you get the transport, which I think is pretty great."*

Brief. The video did the work; the prose just frames it.

### § 05 — What's tested

Three bolded lead-ins. Audiocontrol's "honest about limits" register, but trimmed for the audience:

- **Hardware.** Roland MC-500mkII (1988). Confirmed. Other Roland sequencers in the same family — the original MC-500, the smaller MC-50 — likely work, but I haven't tested them. If you have one and try it, let me know.
- **DAWs.** Logic Pro, Ableton Live, LUNA. If your DAW takes a hardware controller for transport, this is one. If it doesn't, this isn't.
- **Computer.** Mac. The Linux build runs but I haven't tested it against a DAW. No Windows yet.

(No mention of MCU, CoreMIDI, virtual ports. The reader doesn't need to know — it's just a thing you install and it works.)

### § 06 — Get it

Available from GitHub releases. The macOS download is a `.app` you drag into your Applications folder; double-click to run, then point your DAW at it as a control surface.

→ Download: <https://github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol/releases>

What's next, briefly: more vintage gear support, more DAWs verified, more of the panel mapped. If you've got an MC-500mkII and a DAW, try it. If it breaks, file an issue with what gear and what DAW.

(One opt-in pointer for curious readers, in italic at the very end of §06: *"If you want the protocol details — MIDI Song Position, Mackie Control, the bridge architecture — the source is at github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol."* That's the only nod to the implementation in the entire dispatch. Operator's call whether to keep it or cut.)

- **VO transcription:** `/tmp/mc-500-overlay/vo.json` (whisper-cli small.en, 28 segments). Voice and content backbone. - **Demo video:** <https://youtu.be/IIhBlliWr9k> — hero element, above the fold.
- **Operator's reviews (v1, v4 — v4 is the audience reorientation):** the dispatch is for musicians, not engineers. Cut all protocol-speak from the prose. Drop the ASCII diagram. Drop the implementation callout. Drop the Homebrew tap name. Reframe §01 from "hard problem" to "how cool would it be if." Add a screenshot of the control surface in §02. Title applied: *Control Your DAW with this Rock-Solid Roland Sequencer*.
- **Format precedent (revised — narrative dispatch for musicians):** `claude-vs-codex-claude-perspective` for journey-arc shape. The audiocontrol-voice skill stays the spine — sentence-case headers, receipts, honest-about-limits — but the technical density dials down two notches for this audience.

## Open questions for the operator (decide before draft)

1. **Title finalist.** "Rock-Solid Roland Sequencer" version applied. If you want one of the alts (Two Great Things, MC-500mkII Was Already Great, etc.), say so before draft.
2. **Screenshot.** §02 needs an image of the bridge's control / configuration surface. What does it show today? Operator captures + drops the file in the post directory; outline notes the placeholder filename to use.
3. **MC-500 (original, non-mkII) status.** v1's review said "only mkII works (Super MRC OS dependency)." v4's note casually says "MC-500mkII (and, likely, the MC-500)." Reconciliation in §05: confirmed = mkII; *likely* = original MC-500 + MC-50, untested. If the operator has stronger conviction either way, sharpen the language before draft.
4. **§ 04 length.** With the video above the fold, §04 might be redundant. Keep as a 2-paragraph "what you just watched" recap, or fold into §05?
5. **§ 06 protocol-pointer (italic line at the end).** Keep the one-line opt-in pointer for the curious, or cut entirely? Operator said "we don't want to talk about the code at all" — a one-line italic pointer arguably honors that, but if it doesn't, it goes.
6. **Audience stance, double-check.** Should the dispatch occasionally name a DAW feature by name (e.g. "MCU controller" in §02) for musicians who DO know the term, or stay strictly plain-language? Strict plain-language is safer; named-feature is shorter. Operator's call.
